html:
An undersea earthquake near Crete at about sunrise on 21 July 365, and the tsunami it sent across the eastern Mediterranean. Geologists estimate a magnitude of 8 or more.

The quake lifted parts of western Crete by up to about nine metres; old shorelines can still be seen above the sea. Towns in Crete, Greece, Libya and Cyprus were wrecked, and Libyan cities such as Cyrene never fully recovered.

The tsunami hit Alexandria and the Nile Delta. The Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus wrote that the sea first drew back, leaving ships stranded and fish on the mud, then rushed in, flooding the city and throwing ships onto the roofs of houses. Alexandria marked the day each year as a "day of horror" for two centuries. It happened while the Roman Empire was divided between the brothers Valentinian and Valens.
